title: Fighting COVID-19 Misinformation on Social Media: Experimental Evidence for a Scalable Accuracy-Nudge Intervention
overview: Pennycook et al. (2020), Psychological Science 31(7): two online survey experiments on COVID-19 headlines (accuracy vs. sharing; accuracy nudge) and a post hoc item-level analysis.

readiness.note: All four arms can be run. The Study 2 pretest headlines, question and framing are transcribed from sources/study2_materials (txt and docx). Open: how one of the four pretest headlines was assigned (iss_s2_pretest_assign), the original pictures/ledes, and the original instructions.

program.title: Fighting COVID-19 Misinformation on Social Media: Experimental Evidence for a Scalable Accuracy-Nudge Intervention

source.title: Fighting COVID-19 Misinformation on Social Media: Experimental Evidence for a Scalable Accuracy-Nudge Intervention
source.authors: Gordon Pennycook, Jonathon McPhetres, Yunhao Zhang, Jackson G. Lu, and David G. Rand

studies.title: Study 1: accuracy judgments vs. sharing intentions (between participants)
studies.description: 853 analysed U.S. Lucid participants judged either accuracy or sharing of 30 COVID-19 headlines; individual-differences correlates.

studies.title: Study 2: accuracy-nudge experiment on sharing intentions
studies.description: 856 analysed U.S. Lucid participants shared (6-point scale) the same 30 headlines after a control start or after rating one unrelated headline.

studies.title: Item-level analysis across Studies 1 and 2
studies.description: Post hoc correlation between each headline's Study 1 perceived accuracy and its Study 2 treatment effect (r(28)).

fields.label: Method type
fields.value: Two online survey experiments with U.S. adults (Lucid quota sample), randomised between participants, with true and false COVID-19 news headlines as repeated stimuli, plus a post hoc item-level analysis combining both studies.
fields.derivation: Combined from the abstract and the Study 1 and Study 2 method sections.

fields.label: Summary
fields.value: Study 1 compares accuracy judgments with sharing intentions for 15 false and 15 true COVID-19 headlines and relates truth discernment to individual differences. Study 2 tests whether first rating the accuracy of one unrelated headline raises truth discernment in later sharing intentions.
fields.derivation: Condensed from the abstract and the statements of aim for each study.

fields.label: Question
fields.value: Do people share false COVID-19 claims partly because they fail to consider accuracy when deciding what to share, and does a subtle accuracy reminder improve what they are willing to share?
fields.derivation: Rephrased from the abstract and the aims of Studies 1 and 2.

fields.label: Gap
fields.value: It was unclear, however, how (or whether) these results would generalize to COVID-19.

fields.label: Theory
fields.value: According to this account, people generally wish to avoid spreading misinformation and, in fact, are often able to tell truth from falsehood; however, they nonetheless share false and misleading content because the social media context focuses their attention on factors other than accuracy

fields.label: Concepts
fields.value: Truth discernment: the difference in accuracy judgments (or sharing intentions) between true and false headlines.

nodes.title: Study 1 hypothesis: sharing is less truth-discerning than accuracy judgments

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Discernment between true and false COVID-19 headlines is higher when participants judge accuracy than when they decide about sharing (a veracity-by-condition interaction); discernment is also related to analytic cognitive style and science knowledge.
fields.derivation: The paper reports 'As predicted' for the interaction and lists the correlational aims; the statement merges the two passages.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: True and false COVID-19 news headlines; U.S. adults on Lucid; March 2020.
fields.derivation: From the Study 1 aim and sample description.

nodes.title: Study 2 hypothesis: an accuracy nudge raises sharing discernment

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Subtly making the concept of accuracy salient (rating one unrelated headline first) increases the veracity of the COVID-19 headlines people say they would share.
fields.derivation: The paper reports 'As predicted' for the veracity-by-treatment interaction.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Sharing intentions for the 30 Study 1 headlines; control vs. treatment between participants.
fields.derivation: From the Study 2 method.

nodes.title: Item-level expectation: the nudge matters most for headlines seen as clearly true or clearly false

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Given the proposed mechanism, the treatment should change sharing of a headline in proportion to its perceived accuracy.
fields.derivation: Paraphrase of the stated item-level expectation.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Post hoc analysis; Study 1 accuracy ratings are used as a proxy for how accurate Study 2 participants would deem each headline.

fields.label: Setting

fields.label: Support
fields.value: Veracity × treatment β = 0.039, p < .0001; discernment 2.8 times higher in treatment.

fields.label: Mechanism proposed
fields.value: The nudge makes participants more likely to consider accuracy when deciding whether to share.

fields.label: Steps
fields.value: Replay the 30-headline sharing task. Treatment adds the pretest headline first, which cannot be replayed until its headline, question and framing wording are supplied. Other measures are not replayed.

fields.label: Conditions
fields.value: Control is runnable; treatment is blocked by the missing pretest materials.

fields.label: Outcomes
fields.value: 6-point sharing ratings, rescaled to 0-1, sharing discernment and the veracity × treatment interaction (only when both arms exist).

fields.label: Limits
fields.value: Text-only headlines; one prompt per participant containing all 30 headlines; subtle manipulation may behave differently for a language model; hypothetical sharing; no demographic persona; AI agreement with the paper would not show that people behave the same way.

fields.label: Observation unit

fields.label: Aim
fields.value: Show that the treatment effect on sharing of a headline varies with its perceived accuracy.

fields.label: Inputs

fields.label: Result kind
fields.value: reported

fields.label: Reading
fields.value: Headlines more likely to be identified as true were more strongly positively impacted (sharing increases) by the accuracy nudge.

fields.label: Answer
fields.value: The nudge appears to increase attention to whether headlines seem true or not when deciding what to share.
fields.derivation: The paper states this as the authors' hypothesised reading of the correlation.

fields.label: Steps
fields.value: Computed from replayed Study 1 accuracy sessions and replayed Study 2 control and treatment sessions; there is no separate participant task.

fields.label: Roles
fields.value: No participants of its own.

fields.label: Conditions
fields.value: Needs Study 1 accuracy and Study 2 control and treatment arms.

fields.label: Outcomes
fields.value: Correlation across 30 headlines; not ready until the Study 2 treatment arm exists.

fields.label: Limits
fields.value: Depends on the blocked treatment arm; with few simulated participants item means are noisy.

fields.label: Validity
fields.value: Self-reported sharing is supported by evidence that headlines with higher reported sharing likelihood receive more shares on Twitter; the subtle manipulation makes demand effects unlikely.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Evidence is restricted to the United States; the quota sample is not probability based and should not be considered truly nationally representative.

fields.label: Limitations
fields.value: A particular set of true and false COVID-19 headlines; sharing intentions were hypothetical and the accuracy induction was performed in a 'lab' context.

fields.label: Replications reported
fields.value: Pennycook et al. (2020) applied the same accuracy-reminder intervention to political misinformation and replicated the survey results with direct messages on Twitter.

fields.label: Openness
fields.value: Data and materials are on OSF (https://osf.io/7d3xh/); Studies 1 and 2 were preregistered at AsPredicted; the preregistration erroneously planned to cluster standard errors on participant only.

evidence.quote: Across two studies with more than 1,700 U.S. adults recruited online, we present evidence that people share false claims about COVID-19 partly because they simply fail to think sufficiently about whether or not the content is accurate when deciding what to share.
Psychological Science 2020, Vol. 31(7)

According to this account, people generally wish to avoid spreading misinformation and, in fact, are often able to tell truth from falsehood; however, they nonetheless share false and misleading content because the social media context focuses their attention on factors other than accuracy
It was unclear, however, how (or whether) these results would generalize to COVID-19.
Study 1 tested for a dissociation between accuracy judgments and sharing intentions when participants evaluated a set of true and false news headlines about COVID-19.

by evaluating the relationship between truth discernment and analytic cognitive style (as well as examining science knowledge, partisanship, geographic proximity to COVID-19 diagnoses, and the tendency to overuse vs. underuse medical services)
Study 2 experimentally tested whether subtly making the concept of accuracy salient increased the quality of COVID-19 information that people were willing to share online.

In total, 1,143 participants began the study. However, 192 did not indicate using Facebook or Twitter and therefore did not complete the survey. A further 98 participants did not finish the study and were removed. The final sample consisted of 853 participants (mean age = 46 years, age range = 18–
90; 357 men, 482 women, and 14 who responded “other/prefer not to answer”).
This study was run on March 12, 2020. We recruited 1,000 participants using Lucid, an online recruiting source that aggregates survey respondents from many respondent providers
Lucid uses quota sampling to provide a sample that is matched to the U.S. public on age, gender, ethnicity, and geographic region.
Our sample size was based on the following factors: (a) 1,000 is a large sample size for this design, (b) it was within our budget, and (c) it is similar to what was used in past research
we acquired a list of 15 false and 15 true news headlines relating to COVID-19
The false headlines were deemed to be false by authoritative sources
The true headlines came from reliable mainstream media sources.
one of the false headlines (about bats being the source of the virus) was more misleading or unverified than untrue—however, removing this headline did not change our results, and so we retained it.
Headlines were presented in the format of Facebook posts: a picture accompanied by a headline and lede sentence.
Each participant was randomly assigned to one of two conditions. In the accuracy condition, they were asked, “To the best of your knowledge, is the claim in the above headline accurate?” (yes/no).
In the sharing condition, they were asked, “Would you consider sharing this story online (for example, through Facebook or Twitter?)” (yes/no)
We counterbalanced the order of the yes/no options (no/yes vs. yes/no) across participants. Headlines were presented in a random order.
At the end of both surveys, we informed participants which of the headlines were accurate (by re-presenting the true headlines).
Discernment is defined as the difference in accuracy judgments (or sharing intentions) between true and false headlines.
Thus, a higher discernment score indicates a higher sensitivity to truth relative to falsity.

Prior to the news-evaluation task, participants were asked two questions specific to the COVID-19 pandemic. First, they were asked, “How concerned are you about COVID-19 (the new coronavirus)?” which they answered using a sliding scale from 0 (not concerned at all) to 100 (extremely concerned). Second, they were asked “How often do you proactively check the news regarding COVID-19 (the new coronavirus)?” which they answered on a scale from 1 (never) to 5 (very often).

We gave participants a six-item Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT; Frederick, 2005) that consisted of a reworded version of the original three-item test and three items from a nonnumeric version (we excluded the “hole” item; Thomson & Oppenheimer, 2016).
The CRT had acceptable reliability (Cronbach’s α = .69).
Participants also completed a general science-knowledge quiz—as a measure of general background knowledge for scientific issues—that consisted of 17 questions about basic science facts
The scale had acceptable reliability (Cronbach’s α = .77).
We also administered the Medical Maximizer-Minimizer Scale (MMS; Scherer et al., 2016), which measures the
The MMS also had acceptable reliability (Cronbach’s α = .86).
Finally, in addition to various demographic questions, we measured political ideology on both social and fiscal issues, as well as Democrat versus Republican Party alignment.
we added three screener questions that put a subtle instruction in the middle of a block of text.
Screener questions were placed just prior to the news-evaluation and news-sharing tasks, after the CRT, and after the science-knowledge scale and MMS.
To maintain the representativeness of our sample, we followed our preregistered plan to include all participants in our main analyses, regardless of attentiveness.
We conducted all analyses of headline ratings at the level of the rating, using linear regression with robust standard errors clustered on participants and headline.
Ratings and all individual-differences measures were z scored; headline veracity was coded as –0.5 for false and 0.5 for true, and condition was coded as −0.5 for accuracy and 0.5 for sharing.

The coefficient on headline veracity indicates overall level of discernment (the difference between responses to true vs. false headlines), and the interaction between condition and headline veracity indicates the extent to which discernment differed between the experimental conditions.
Our main analyses used linear probability models instead of logistic regression because the coefficients are more readily interpretable.

All relationships reported below were robust to including controls for age, gender, education (college degree or higher vs. less than college degree), ethnicity (White vs. non-White), and all interactions among controls, veracity, and condition.

As predicted, we observed a significant interaction between headline veracity and condition, β = −0.126, F(1, 25586) = 42.24, p < .0001, indicating that discernment was higher for accuracy judgments than sharing intentions

In other words, veracity had a much bigger impact on accuracy judgments, Cohen’s d = 0.657, 95% confidence interval (CI) = [0.477, 0.836], F(1, 25586) = 42.24, p < .0001, than on sharing intentions, d = 0.121, 95% CI = [0.030, 0.212], F(1, 25586) = 6.74, p = .009.
In particular, for false headlines, 32.4% more people were willing to share the headlines than rated them as accurate.

We found that scores on the CRT were positively related to both accuracy discernment and sharing discernment, as revealed by the interactions between CRT score and veracity, F(1, 25582) = 34.95, p < .0001, and F(1, 25582) = 4.98, p = .026, respectively. However, the relationship was significantly stronger for accuracy, as indicated by the three-way interaction among CRT score, veracity, and condition, F (1, 25582) = 14.68, p = .0001.

Like CRT score, science knowledge was positively correlated with both accuracy discernment, F(1, 25552) = 32.80, p < .0001, and sharing discernment, F(1, 25552) = 10.02, p = .002, but much more so for accuracy, as revealed by the three-way interaction among science knowledge, veracity, and condition, F (1, 25552) = 7.59, p = .006.

In particular, science knowledge was negatively correlated with belief in false headlines and positively correlated with belief in true headlines, whereas science knowledge was negatively correlated with sharing of false headlines and uncorrelated with sharing of true headlines (for effect sizes, see Table 1).

This study was run from March 13 to March 15, 2020. Following the same sample-size considerations as in Study 1, we recruited 1,000 participants using Lucid. In total, 1,145 participants began the study. However, 177 did not indicate using Facebook or Twitter and therefore did not complete the survey. A further 112 participants did not complete the study. The final sample consisted of 856 participants (mean age = 47 years, age range = 18–86; 385 men, 463 women, and 8 who responded “other/prefer not to answer”).

Each participant was randomly assigned to one of two conditions. In the control condition, they began the news-sharing task as in Study 1. In the treatment condition, they rated the accuracy of a single headline (unrelated to COVID-19) before beginning the news-sharing task; following Pennycook et al. (2020), we framed this as being for a pretest.
Each participant saw one of four possible headlines, all politically neutral and unrelated to COVID-19 (see https://osf.io/7d3xh/ for materials).
An advantage of this design is that the manipulation is subtle and not explicitly linked to the main task.
Participants were shown the same headlines as for Study 1 and (as in the sharing condition of Study 1) were asked about their willingness to share the headlines on social media.

In this case, however, we sought to increase the sensitivity of the measure by asking, “If you were to see the above on social media, how likely would you be to share it?” which they answered on a 6-point scale from 1 (extremely unlikely) to 6 (extremely likely).
All of the additional measures included in Study 1 were also included in Study 2.
The same screener questions included in Study 1 were also included in Study 2.

All analyses were conducted at the level of the rating, using linear regression with robust standard errors clustered on participants and headline. Sharing intentions were rescaled such that 1 on the 6-point Likert scale was 0, and 6 on the 6-point Likert scale was 1.
As predicted, we observed a significant positive interaction between headline veracity and treatment, β = 0.039, F(1, 25623) = 17.88, p < .0001; the treatment increased sharing discernment

although participants in the control condition were not significantly more likely to say that they would share true headlines compared with false headlines, d = 0.050, 95% CI = [−0.033, 0.133], F(1, 25623) = 1.41, p = .24, in the treatment condition, sharing intentions for true headlines were significantly higher than for false headlines, d = 0.142, 95% CI = [0.049, 0.235], F (1, 25623) = 8.89, p = .003.
Quantitatively, sharing discernment (the difference in sharing likelihood of true relative to false headlines) was 2.8 times higher in the treatment condition compared with the control condition.
the treatment effect on sharing discernment was not significantly moderated by CRT performance, science knowledge, partisanship, distance to the nearest epicenter, or MMS score
The treatment effect was also robust to excluding the few headlines that did not contain clear claims of fact or that were political in nature

Because participants in Study 2 did not rate the accuracy of the COVID-19-related headlines, we used average Study 1 ratings as a proxy for how accurate participants in Study 2 would likely deem the headlines to be.
Given this mechanism, the extent to which the treatment increases or decreases sharing of a given headline should reflect the underlying perceptions of the headline’s accuracy.
Headlines that were more likely to be identified as true (on the basis of Study 1 data) were more strongly positively impacted (sharing increases) by nudging people to consider accuracy.
Put differently, participants were far less discerning if they were asked about whether they would share a headline on social media than if they were asked about its accuracy.

neutral intervention nearly tripled participants’ level of discernment between sharing true and sharing false headlines.
our results suggest that partisanship is not, apparently, the key factor distracting people from considering accuracy on social media.
First, our evidence is restricted to the United States and therefore needs to be tested elsewhere in the world.

Next, although our sample was quota matched to the U.S. population on age, gender, ethnicity, and region, it was not obtained via probability sampling and therefore should not be considered truly nationally representative.
We also used a particular set of true and false headlines about COVID-19.
Finally, our sharing intentions were hypothetical, and our experimental accuracy induction was performed in a “lab” context.
